The announcements were made earlier today on MLB Network. Alonso earned the honor for the seventh time in his career and second time this season after winning his first award in the AL with the Orioles on August 17th. He previously won five times during his tenure with the Ne
item.content:encoded:
First baseman Pete Alonso of the Baltimore Orioles has been named the American League Player of the Week, and third baseman Nolan Arenado of the Arizona Diamondbacks has been selected the National League Player of the Week. The announcements were made earlier today on MLB Network.
Alonso earned the honor for the seventh time in his career and second time this season after winning his first award in the AL with the Orioles on August 17th. He previously won five times during his tenure with the New York Mets, including June 24, 2019; September 26, 2022; July 30, 2023; April 15, 2024; and June 9, 2025. Alonso is the 12th player ever to garner honors in at least five consecutive seasons, regardless of team or league, joining Hall of Famer Vladimir Guerrero (8 seasons, 1998-2005); Manny Ramirez (7 seasons, 1997-2003); Arenado (6 seasons, 2014-2019); Aaron Judge (6 seasons, 2020-2025); George Bell (5 seasons, 1986-1990); Miguel Cabrera (5 seasons, 2012-2016); Hall of Famer Andre Dawson (5 seasons, 1987-1991); Carlos Delgado (5 seasons, 2000-2004); Clayton Kershaw (5 seasons, 2011-2015); Albert Pujols (5 seasons, 2005-2009); and Gary Sheffield (5 seasons, 1992-96). Arenado earned his ninth career award and first as a member of the Diamondbacks, marking Arizona’s fourth award of the year in addition to his teammates Ildemaro Vargas (April 27th); Ketel Marte (May 26th) and Corbin Carroll (August 17th). Arenado previously won six times as a member of the Colorado Rockies between 2014-2019 and twice as a member of the St. Louis Cardinals in 2022, including August 24, 2014; June 28, 2015; April 18, 2016; July 24, 2017; June 25, 2018; May 27, 2019; April 11, 2022; and August 8, 2022. He is the 31st player with at least nine awards in his career and just the eighth with at least nine awards in the National League, joining Barry Bonds (15); Pujols (13); Hall of Famer Mike Piazza (12); Sammy Sosa (11); Freddie Freeman (10); Hall of Famer Tony Gwynn (10); and Sheffield (9).
- The 31-year-old hit .389 (7-for-18) with five homers, eight RBI, three walks, eight runs scored, a 1.222 slugging percentage and a .500 on-base percentage across five contests.
- The Tampa, Florida native led the Majors in homers, slugging, OPS (1.722) and total bases (22); ranked second in runs scored; tied for third in RBI; and tied for fifth in on-base percentage.
- The five-time All-Star opened his week with a two-homer game against the Blue Jays on Monday and hit a pair of longballs in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium on Friday. Alonso now has 29 career multi-homer games which are third-most in the Majors since his debut in 2019 behind only Aaron Judge (40 G) and Kyle Schwarber (36 G).
- The 2019 Jackie Robinson NL Rookie of the Year also slugged a home run in the first game of a doubleheader on Wednesday against Toronto as he finished his year with 43 homers and 113 RBI. Per Elias, he became the first player since RBI became official in 1920 to lead the AL and NL in RBI for a single season after he led the NL with 131 RBI in 2022. Additionally, he is the eighth Orioles player to lead the league in RBI and the first since Chris Davis had 138 RBI in 2013.
- The 2025 Silver Slugger crossed the 40-homer threshold with his two-homer game on Monday, marking his fourth season of at least 40 home runs, joining 2019 (53 HR); 2022 (40 HR); and 2023 (46 HR). His 43 homers are third-most by a Baltimore player in their first season with the club, behind Hall of Famer Frank Robinson (49 HR in 1966) and Mark Trumbo (47 HR in 2016). Alonso, who has played in 577 consecutive games since June 18, 2023, became the first Oriole to start every game of a season since Jonathan Schoop in 2016.
- The 35-year-old hit .435 (10-for-23) with three homers, eight RBI, two doubles, two walks, seven runs scored, a stolen base, a .913 slugging percentage and a .519 on-base percentage in six games.
- The Newport Beach, California native tied for second in total bases (21) and hits; ranked third in on-base percentage and OPS (1.432); tied for third in slugging, RBI and runs scored; and tied for fifth in batting average.
- The eight-time All-Star slugged a homer on Tuesday and Thursday at Colorado before also going deep on Friday at San Diego, marking his 30th homer of the year. It marked the eighth time in his career that he hit at least 30 homers, and his eight seasons of at least 30 home runs are third-most by a primary third baseman (min. 100 GS at 3B in season), behind only Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12 seasons of 30+ HR) and Eddie Mathews (10 seasons of 30+ HR).
- The 10-time Rawlings Gold Glover and six-time Platinum Glove Award winner finished his season on a 13-game hitting streak that dates back to September 13th, and he hit safely in 18 of his final 20 games of the season. During the stretch, he slashed .420/.463/.840 with six homers, 16 RBI and a 1.303 OPS. Arenado’s hitting streak is the fourth-longest by a Diamondbacks player to end a season, trailing only Paul Goldschmidt (19 G in 2013); Chad Tracy (14 G in 2005); and Tony Womack (14 G in 1999).
- The five-time Silver Slugger reached base safely in each of his last 21 games, matching Luis Gonzalez (2001) for the longest streak to end a season in franchise history. Overall, his 21-game on-base streak is the fifth-longest single season on-base streak of his career behind a 30-game streak in 2014, a 25-gamer in 2024 and a pair of 24-gamers in 2024 and 2018.
Other noteworthy NL performances last week included starting pitcher Jared Jones (1-0, 0.00 ERA, 2 GS, 11.0 IP, 2 H, 0 BB, 14 SO) of the Pittsburgh Pirates; starting pitcher Eury Pérez (1-0, 0.00 ERA, 1 GS, 10.0 IP, 1 H, 1 BB, 11 SO) of the Miami Marlins; infielder Bryson Stott (.474, 2 RBI, 6 2B, 5 BB, 4 R, .789 SLG, .583 OBP) of the Philadelphia Phillies; rookie outfielder Carson Benge (.440, 1 HR, 4 RBI, 3 2B, 3 BB, 5 R, .680 SLG, .500 OBP) of the New York Mets; second baseman Brice Turang (.360, 2 HR, 7 RBI, 3 2B, 1 BB, 5 R, .720 SLG) and outfielder Jackson Chourio (.471, 1 HR, 5 RBI, 3 BB, 7 R, 2 SB, .647 SLG, .550 OBP) of the Milwaukee Brewers; the 2026 Tony Gwynn NL Batting Champion, catcher Gabriel Moreno (.400, 1 HR, 8 RBI, 1 2B, 1 3B, 2 BB, 5 R, .600 SLG, .435 OBP) of the Arizona Diamondbacks; and utilityman Mauricio Dubón (.368, 1 HR, 3 RBI, 1 BB, 3 R, 1 SB, .526 SLG, .400 OBP) of the Atlanta Braves.
Other noteworthy AL performances last week included rookie outfielder Lucas Spence (.333, 4 HR, 9 RBI, 1 2B, 1 3B, 4 BB, 5 R, 1.167 SLG, .455 OBP), the 2026 AL Rod Carew Batting Champion, All-Star outfielder Yordan Alvarez (.375, 2 HR, 7 RBI, 2 2B, 4 BB, 7 R, .708 SLG, .483 OBP) and first baseman Christian Walker (.348, 4 HR, 7 RBI, 1 2B, 3 BB, 7 R, .913 SLG, .407 OBP); utilityman Luke Keaschall (.381, 1 HR, 6 RBI, 2 2B, 1 3B, 3 BB, 10 R, 1 SB, .905 SLG, .462 OBP) of the Minnesota Twins; closer Cade Smith (0.00 ERA, 3 G, 2 SV, 2.2 IP, 0 H, 1 BB, 4 SO) of the Cleveland Guardians; first baseman Vinnie Pasquantino (.333, 3 HR, 9 RBI, 2 2B, 1 BB, 6 R, .792 SLG, .385 OBP) and outfielder Jac Caglianone (.455, 4 RBI, 5 2B, 4 R, .682 SLG, .455 OBP) of the Kansas City Royals; outfielder Wade Meckler (.435, 2 RBI, 1 2B, 3 BB, 3 R, .565 SLG, .480 OBP) of the Los Angeles Angels; and All-Star first baseman Munetaka Murakami (.292, 3 HR, 7 RBI, 2 2B, 2 BB, 5 R, .750 SLG, .370 OBP) and second baseman Chase Meidroth (.615, 1 HR, 5 RBI, 2 2B, 1 BB, 3 R, 1.000 SLG, .643 OBP) of the Chicago White Sox.
Atlanta Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. earned his fourth career Play of the Week Award, after previously winning on August 19, 2019; August 8, 2022; and July 21, 2025. Overall, it is the 13th honor for the Braves since the inception of the award in 2019 with Acuña’s four awards joined by honors to Charlie Culberson (7/8/2019); Nick Markakis (7/15/2019); Adam Duvall (9/8/2020); Tyler Matzek (5/10/2021); a joint award to Ozzie Albies and Orlando Arcia (7/3/2023); Austin Riley (8/19/2024); Michael Harris II (9/3/2024); Jurickson Profar (8/11/2025); and Jim Jarvis (5/11/2026). With no outs and the Braves leading the Marlins 1-0 in the second inning, Heriberto Hernández hit a ball towards the wall as Acuña made a leaping catch to take away extra-bases. Additional Play of the Week candidates included Javier Sanoja’s fantastic play to keep the game alive; Henry Bolte’s diving catch; Bryan Reynolds’ diving catch and throw to second for a double play; Ceddanne Rafaela’s diving catch; and Jase Bowen’s leaping catch at the wall.

item.title: [The Baltimore Banner] 5 takeaways from the Orioles' end-of-season press conference
item.dc:creator: Andy Kostka

item.content:encoded:
Join the dugout. Sign up here for Orioles updates in your inbox.
A day after the Orioles season ended with a rainout, not a game, president of baseball operations Mike Elias said he and the rest of the organization are “tired” of losing baseball. Elias thanked the fans for “hanging in there with us” and said Baltimore will undergo a full organizational review to improve the team’s fortunes.
These are five takeaways from Baltimore’s end-of-season press conference with Elias and manager Craig Albernaz.
Execution is the buzzword
The reasons the Orioles finished 79-82 in this 161-game season are multifold, but the conversations Albernaz had with players in one-on-one meetings all included the same word.
“Execution,” Albernaz said.
The Orioles didn’t execute well enough all year. Baltimore led the majors with 88 unearned runs, and the club lost far too many winnable games due to mistakes. Albernaz often preached needing to do the “little things” correctly, and as he enters his second year, there will be renewed focus on that front.
Of course, Albernaz made that a point of emphasis in his first spring training, as well. He told the group then that “they’re talented,” but “everyone is talented in this game.”
“At the end of the day, we have to make sure that we do the little things right and the fundamentals right, and it really is more of a mental piece than actually physical,” Albernaz said. “Everyone is physically capable of doing it. It’s just the consistency of mentally locking in on every single pitch, knowing what you’re supposed to do with the ball, or et cetera. So, for us, it’s really drilling down on that mental capacity of each guy, and for us as a coaching staff, if there’s any shortcomings or anything that’s lost in translation, we have to be there to support the players.”
In conversations with multiple players over the last few days of the season, this was an oft-repeated phrase from them, too. Infielder Jackson Holliday pointed to his dropped popup against the Colorado Rockies as an example of a lack of execution, and that directly led to a loss. Shortstop Gunnar Henderson said the failure to do “little things” consistently well is what led to a losing record in one-run games this year.
“It’s executing our game plan when the hitter is in the box,” Albernaz said. “Executing our game plan when we’re on the mound. Executing on defense, baserunning. Execution is the biggest thing. And that is something that we’re going to be diving into and drilling hard this offseason and then looking forward in spring training.”
What is up with Gunnar Henderson’s wrist?
After what turned out to be the final game of the season, shortstop Gunnar Henderson admitted, with reluctance, that he dealt with a wrist injury for about half the season. He declined to share the exact details but said he will not require any surgery.
It’s a possible explanation for why Henderson’s season went as poorly — by his standards — as it did. The 25-year-old produced a career-worst .715 on-base-plus-slugging percentage, down from the heights of .893 in 2024.
“I really don’t like making excuses, because everybody’s banged up at this point in the year. But yeah, I had a little [right] wrist issue going on,” Henderson said. “But I felt like bat knob changes helped that out. So it was just minor, getting that a little bit better.”
Henderson changed his bat handle from a traditional knob to an axe handle. The results didn’t markedly improve. He produced a career-low .232 average against fastballs.
Still, Elias credited Henderson with the way he powered through and stayed on the field for 158 games.
“He did a great job navigating everything,” Elias said. “It’s part of baseball, and I think the organization and Gunnar handled that particular situation about as well as you could.”
Albernaz said there were daily check-ins with Henderson to assess his availability, but he admitted that “sometimes you just have to just let him be, because he’s intense and he’s as competitive as anyone I’ve been around.”
The balance, of course, is whether playing with a nagging injury is a case of diminishing returns.
“I know it wasn’t the results that he wanted, but you look up and he had an over .700 OPS and 24 homers,” Albernaz said. “It’s still productive for a shortstop at this level. So, I’m proud of Gunnar and the way he went about his business this year.”
An expanding front office
The Orioles’ front office has already undergone some changes. Sig Mejdal is no longer overseeing the analytics department. Matt Blood, the vice president of player and staff development, departed the organization.
Elias is hoping to build out the front office with outside voices, especially given that he estimated that Baltimore’s front office size is 29th out of 30 in Major League Baseball. The Orioles are restarting a search for a general manager under Elias, and a source with direct knowledge of the search said Baltimore would like to find someone with a player development background to complement Elias’ scouting history.
“With our ownership group now, we have a good opportunity to sort of participate in that growth a little bit more than we’ve been doing,” he said. “And there’s parts of our baseball operation that I think I could use some different voices and ideas in more than others. I don’t know that I want to get into it here on the stage, but you’ll probably be able to see as these hires come in where we’re looking for some impact.”
Analytics are part and parcel to modern baseball
The discourse surrounding the modern approach of analytics can revolve around how the Orioles rely on it too much. It’s an idea mentioned by former Orioles shortstop Mike Bordick on 105.7 The Fan last week.
In reality, analytics are a part of baseball’s present and future, and that isn’t going to change.
“It’s clearly an enormous part of success in this sport nowadays,” Elias said. “It can, I think, get unfairly attacked when a team is not being successful because it, by nature, presents counterintuitive information. That’s the whole point of it, and I totally understand and appreciate all that. And my roots as a person in baseball, over 20 years in Major League Baseball, is as being a subjective evaluator that does not provide analytical information but marries it with stuff that’s more traditional and more intuitive.”
Pete Alonso was a smashing success, but the Orioles will pick their spots in free agency
Pete Alonso, fresh off his five-year, $155 million contract, was a huge success in his first year for the Orioles. He became the first player in MLB history to lead the National League and American League in RBIs in separate seasons after he posted 113, along with a league-leading 43 homers.
But Elias didn’t commit to pursuing that level of free agent each offseason.
“We have owners now that really have the ability to do that, and they’ve already flexed that,” Elias said. “We were in a position this offseason to pursue a player like Pete, and we did it pretty aggressively, and so far, really happy with that. … I’m glad that the experience we’re having with Pete has been so rewarding so far because it is important to be able to pursue and attract big free agents when it makes sense.”
Elias said the scouting department will determine when the Orioles have the “confidence” in a large free agent, “that’s how we’ll pursue it.”

item.title: [ocregister.com] Dodgers’ Kyle Tucker can salvage his season with strong October
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — October can be a powerful stain remover. How much of a disappointing regular season can be washed away by a productive postseason – or just a key contribution at a pivotal moment? “Everything,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we’ve seen it with Kiké (Hernandez). item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — October can be a powerful stain remover.
How much of a disappointing regular season can be washed away by a productive postseason – or just a key contribution at a pivotal moment?
“Everything,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we’ve seen it with Kiké (Hernandez). I think we’ve seen it with other guys … Chris Taylor has done it. We’re about winning championships, so I think the media, the fan base, if you perform at the right time, all is forgotten.”
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman agrees.
“Oh, for sure,” Friedman said. “Like if you said, Player X can have a down regular season as compared to his previous performance but a really good October – I couldn’t pick it across the board because then we wouldn’t get a bye. But with one-offs, I would absolutely take that.”
This is an expensive one-off. Neither Hernandez nor Taylor carried the weight of a four-year, $240 million contract before emerging as postseason heroes.
Kyle Tucker signed that contract with the Dodgers last winter with the second-highest annual average value in MLB history behind teammate Shohei Ohtani. Then he went out and had the worst season of his career. Across the board, his slash line of .233/.330/.385 and OPS of .715 were the lowest since he played just 22 major-league games with the Houston Astros in 2019. His home run total (17), RBIs (70) and total bases (208) were the lowest in his five full seasons in the majors.
It’s the kind of performance when tied to that salary that would have made Tucker the target of fan vitriol and constant negative coverage by the media in many other MLB cities. It’s the kind of mistake that has sunk front offices in the past. With the Dodgers, though, Tucker just receded into the background of another 100-win season.
“I don’t know,” Tucker said when asked if he realized how differently his season would have landed had he signed with another team. “If I signed somewhere else and had a great year, everything could have been a different situation so I don’t really think or worry about what could have been. I just worry about where I’m at.”
And Tucker maintains that $60 million price tag on his season never weighed on him.
“I just show up and try to do my job,” he said. “I don’t really think about what I’m getting paid or what anyone else is getting paid.
“I guess (he was subject to less scrutiny on the Dodgers’ star-filled roster). I just show up. I don’t worry about all the other stuff. I just show up and play for the Dodgers and try to win for us.”
With few exceptions, Tucker showed up with no outward signs of the struggle or disappointment he might have been experiencing over the course of a season that didn’t meet anyone’s expectations. His low-key nature left reporters probing for signs that Tucker was affected by his performance, turning post-game interviews into mental health checks filled with questions about how Tucker was handling the disappointment, what he felt was behind his dismal home-and-road splits, who he turned to for support or where he found signs of hope in the darkness of a sub-.230 batting average.
“I don’t know,” Tucker said, laughing at that suggestion and turning the questions back on the reporter. “‘I’m good. How are you doing?’”
On the field, Tucker has been doing much better – a positive sign for a redemptive postseason as the team begins preparations for a best-of-five National League Division Series against Atlanta or Philadelphia that will begin Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
September was by far Tucker’s best month of his first season with the Dodgers. He hit .262 with an .889 OPS and six home runs.
“My recent play is more what I expected from myself,” said Tucker, crediting work with the hitting coaches to stabilize and improve his swing path for the September success.
“I just feel like my swing path and my approach and everything is in a really good spot. I just try to keep that going every single day and not really steer away from it. Whatever works works and try to keep doing it,” he said.
“Just trying to keep my swing path in the zone early and long. I’ve just been able to maintain that for awhile now. It’s just been hit and miss throughout the year and I wasn’t able to find something consistent that works.”
Before he discovered that and had his most productive month, there were questions about whether Tucker might be platooned or even benched during the postseason. In late August, Roberts said he addressed that speculation head on with Tucker, telling him “I’m going to ride or die” with you.
“He’s not much for reaction, so I think that he processed it. I think he was pleased,” Roberts said.
“It’s been fun to watch Kyle build some confidence (in September). … You can see him just freed up a little bit. He’s been working hard this whole year, and he’s been in it. And I give him a lot of credit for continuing to persevere and (I) expect the best of him to be at the end of the season.”
If that season ends with a World Series championship, Tucker expects that to be all anyone remembers about his first season as a Dodger.
“I mean, that’s why we play, to try and win a World Series,” he said. “Obviously the fan base expects that out of us. We expect that out of ourselves too.
“If you win a World Series no one cares. As long as you win the last game of the year, that’s all that matters.”

item.title: [MLB.com] Postseason FAQ: What's next for Dodgers?
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: For the 14th straight year, the Dodgers are postseason-bound. Winners of three of the past six World Series, the Dodgers are looking to continue their reign. The back-to-back defending champions are bidding for the Major Leagues' first three-peat since the Yankees won three straight titles from 1998-2000. The Dodgers, the No. 2 seed in the National League, are just about at full strength now that the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki have returned from the injured list, but ther
item.content:encoded:
For the 14th straight year, the Dodgers are postseason-bound.
Winners of three of the past six World Series, the Dodgers are looking to continue their reign. The back-to-back defending champions are bidding for the Major Leagues' first three-peat since the Yankees won three straight titles from 1998-2000.
The Dodgers, the No. 2 seed in the National League, are just about at full strength now that the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki have returned from the injured list, but there are several other compelling storylines to follow before the postseason.
Here's what to watch as the NL West-champion Dodgers forge their path back to the Fall Classic:
What could the postseason roster look like?
The strength of the Dodgers' pitching staff is the rotation, so expect them to carry more starters than they need and get creative with using some of them in relief. Manager Dave Roberts indicated that the team may carry only 12 pitchers to make room for an additional position player on the bench in the NL Division Series.
It may be premature to pencil in Josue De Paula, as the organization’s top prospect has played in only 11 big league games. But the Dodgers liked what they saw, and he could be an impact lefty bat off the bench.
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
First baseman (1): Freddie Freeman
Second baseman (1): Tommy Edman
Shortstop (1): Mookie Betts
Third baseman (1): Max Muncy
Outfielders (3): Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker
Utility/bench (3): Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim
Two-way player (1): Shohei Ohtani
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Relievers (9): Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Roki Sasaki, Kris Bubic, Brock Stewart
When does the postseason begin?
The NL Division Series begin on Saturday.
Who could be the Dodgers' NLDS opponent? 
The Dodgers won their 13th NL West title in the past 14 seasons and secured a first-round bye, so they will play the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and the Phillies.
Against which teams do the Dodgers have home-field advantage?
The Dodgers have home-field advantage over every team in the postseason field except the Brewers, who finished the regular season with the best record in the Majors.
What will the postseason rotation look like?
Yamamoto, Skubal, Snell and Glasnow make up this year's Big Four. The rotation order is yet to be determined. One consideration is that Yamamoto is accustomed to starting on at least five days' rest, whereas the other three are comfortable starting on four days' rest. That makes Yamamoto likely to start Game 1 of the NLDS because he would be available for a potential Game 5 on his normal rest. 
What's the latest on Ohtani's status?
Ohtani was activated from the 15-day IL and hit in the Dodgers' final five games, going 5-for-21 (.238) with eight strikeouts and one walk. Roberts described the performance as Ohtani showing some rust and said the team does not have any health concerns with him. 
Which injured players could return?   
The Dodgers hope that Henriquez, who has emerged as an important leverage arm, can return for the postseason after his regular season came to a premature end due to lower back discomfort. He will face hitters during the bye week, and as long as he comes away feeling good, he will be activated for the NLDS.
Which roster spots may be up for grabs?
The final spot on the bench is far from set in stone. The Dodgers could carry De Paula, but Dalton Rushing, Alex Call and Hyeseong Kim are additional options. This decision could come down to whether they want to use that bench spot on a potential impact bat or someone who brings enhanced speed and/or defense to the table. If L.A. carries fewer than 13 pitchers, that would open an additional bench spot.
The bullpen should also have some openings. If Henriquez does not recover in time for the postseason, that opens an additional spot. Justin Wrobleski, Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan were starters for most of the season, but they will be relief options in the postseason. But Wrobleski was inconsistent in the second half, and the Dodgers have other left-handers who may be more reliable in leverage, such as Bubic.
Who will close out games?
Díaz was supposed to resolve the Dodgers' ninth-inning troubles, but he has only added to them in his first year in L.A. Since returning from the IL, he has looked much better, which could have him back in the mix to close out games. The Dodgers may be more likely to play the matchups instead of going with a set closer in the postseason. Based on regular-season performance, Scott and Henriquez are two of the top options to pitch in save situations. Perhaps Sasaki could reprise his postseason closer role if needed.

item.title: [fansided.com] Evaluating the Hall of Fame trajectories of Shohei Ohtani and MLB’s postseason stars
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman

item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

item.title: [fansided.com] Ranking the top 26 MLB free agents available this offseason, starting with Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: Robert Murray

item.content:encoded:
A common debate that I’ve had with league executives is how many $100+-million contracts will actually be handed out this winter.
Some say one. Others say two. Others say three. But what everyone can agree on is that this is a weaker-than-usual free agent class. The clear headliner is Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Tarik Skubal; after that, industry sources have a wide range of views as to how good this group is — and who should be considered the best non-Skubal target.
I've weighed in with my own take below. Here’s a look at the top 26 free agents of the coming winter, with educated guesses as to who will (and won't) opt out of their contracts in some cases.
1. LHP Tarik Skubal
Skubal is the consensus top free agent in the class, and the expectation is that just about all of the big-market teams will be bidding on the superstar left-hander. He should top the current record for a free-agent contract given to a starting pitcher, currently held by Yoshinobu Yamamoto at $325 million. One source predicted that Skubal could try to sign before the lockout to try and get ahead of CBA uncertainty, though his agent Scott Boras is known for waiting out the market.
2. OF Seiya Suzuki
Suzuki, 32, is one of the top bats on the market and has improved defensively in the corner outfield. He’s hit at least 20 home runs in four consecutive seasons, with a career-high 32 in 2025, and will have plenty of interest from offense-needy teams — with an early report already linking the slugger to the Toronto Blue Jays.
3. OF Randy Arozarena
Arozarena is Mr. Consistent. He’s posted six consecutive 20-20 seasons and he had a very strong contract year in 2026, hitting .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs and 79 RBI. He’s earned a multi-year deal, one that eventually should top Teoscar Hernandez’s three-year, $66 million pact with the Dodgers.
4. 3B/OF Teruaki Sato (Hanshin Tigers)
Sato, 27, is hitting .315/.392/.620 with 37 home runs and 100 RBI this season in NPB. The third baseman/outfielder is the best power hitter on the market and is in the running to win the MVP award in Japan. It’s difficult to predict what he will ultimately sign for, especially after Munataki Murakami’s surprising free agency last year, but he will have a wide market of suitors.
5. LHP Trevor Rogers
Rogers, 28, has had an up-and-down tenure with the Orioles, from being traded to the franchise in 2024 to getting optioned to the Minors after posting a 7.11 ERA in four appearances. He then had a 1.81 ERA last season and has followed it up with a 4.03 ERA this year, though he once again finished strong with a 3.52 ERA in 79.1 innings in the second half.
6. RHP Freddy Peralta
It’s been a roller-coaster year for Peralta, who once seemed like a lock to sign a nine-figure contract but strugged enough with the Mets that a one-year deal seemed plausible, if not likely. Now, he’s bounced back with the Tampa Bay Rays, posting a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts, and one league source texted recently that he “will do just fine” in free agency. One additional note: Peralta is regarded as one of the best clubhouse guys in baseball. He is universally loved by every one of his teammates, past and present.
7. C Ryan Jeffers
At one point, Jeffers felt like a lock to be traded ahead of the Aug. 3 deadline, and he ultimately stayed with the Minnesota Twins. While he’s not the best defensive catcher in baseball, his offense more than makes up for it, and he hit .256/.353/.461 with an .814 OPS, 14 home runs and 56 RBI this season. With how many teams need catching, he seems primed to turn down the qualifying offer in favor of a multi-year deal this winter.
8. RHP Michael King
King is not technically a free agent, but we’ll put him here anyway. The 31-year-old has been tremendous for the Padres with a 3.21 ERA in 32 starts. There were concerns about his durability last winter, hence why he signed an opt out-heavy contract to return to San Diego (he had an in-division offer he strongly considered, too). And it should be noted that despite those concerns, his arm has relatively little wear and tear across eight Major League seasons (just 679.2 career innings).
9. 2B Brandon Lowe
I was talking on the phone with a high-ranking rival executive recently when Lowe’s name was brought up. “He’s a f***ing beast, bro.” He’s not wrong! Lowe hit 35 home runs with 96 RBI while slashing .260/.331/.493 in his first year in Pittsburgh. What’s been most noteworthy is his improvement defensively. He’s going to do very well in free agency, with plenty of teams eagerly awaiting the chance to sign the free-agent infielder.
10. LHP Adrian Morejon
Morejon was mentioned plenty at the trade deadline, but what was not mentioned much was that the Padres and A.J. Preller love the left-hander. They did not want to part with him and mess with their bullpen unless the offer was truly too good to pass up. A return to San Diego should not be ruled out. But a player with Morejon’s production (a 2.83 ERA in 76 appearances) while only being 27 years old will have an extensive market.
11. 2B Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Chisholm Jr. had a breakout season last year with the Yankees when he hit 31 home runs. His numbers have come down a bit in 2026, with the infielder hitting .231/.312/.399 with 19 home runs and 55 RBI. Still, he’s only 28 years old, younger than Suzuki and Arozarena, and has been to the postseason four years in a row. He’ll be one of the most talked-about free agents of the offseason, but the expectation I have from talking to folks across baseball is he’ll have a good market.
12. RHP David Bednar
For years, Bednar has been one of the best relievers in baseball. He was the subject of consistent trade interest with the Pirates, who ultimately traded him to the Yankees at the 2025 deadline. He’s been very good in the Bronx, with a 2.39 ERA in 86 games since being traded. He’s proven that he can pitch in the biggest of markets, which will only bolster his value. At only 31 years old, he’s primed for a lucrative multi-year contract.
13. OF Ian Happ
Happ, 31, has been one of the most consistent players in baseball across his 10-year career. He’s hit over 21 home runs in each of the last four seasons. His numbers this year declined, however, as he hit only .218/.326/.412 with 24 home runs and 68 RBI. He’s striking out more and his OPS+ finished at 103, noticeably lower than his career average of 114.
14. LHP Foster Griffin
Griffin was perhaps the steal of the offseason, with the Washington Nationals signing the left-hander for one year and $5.5 million. He posted a 3.06 ERA in 22 starts with the Nats and was eventually traded to the Guardians for multiple prospects at the deadline. He finished the year with a 3.60 ERA in 31 starts, and is in line for a multi-year contract this winter. He’s been a tremendous success story coming after coming back from pitching in Japan for three seasons.
15. 2B Luis Arraez
Arraez has always been one of the best hitters in baseball; his defense has been what has given teams hesitation. Those concerns are no more as he’s morphed into an above-average second baseman after working with Ron Washington in San Francisco. If healthy, he’ll have a real chance at a multi-year contract this offseason after slashing .310/.345/.419 with an .801 OPS.
16. RHP Sonny Gray
Gray is not technically a free agent, but he has a $30 million mutual option. Mutual options are never picked up, though, and if he becomes available, he will be heavily in demand — and a contract in the three-year, $75 million range would make plenty of sense. But he did recently tell Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com that he would retire “in a heartbeat” if his family indicated a desire for him to hang up his cleats. He clearly still has more in the tank, but this will be a situation to monitor that could affect the rest of the pitching market.
17. RHP Casey Mize
Mize, 29, appeared primed for a lucrative multi-year contract earlier this season when he had a 2.70 ERA in 16 starts with the Detroit Tigers. Since being traded to the San Diego Padres, he has a 7.46 ERA and a 25/19 strikeout-to-walk ratio. He could be a strong candidate for a short-term deal so he can have a better platform season and hit the market again after 2027 in hopes for a long-term contract.
18. LHP Robbie Ray
Ray, 34, is surely looking at a short-term contract at this stage of his career. He was consistent with the Giants, with a 3.54 ERA in 60 starts, but has struggled with the Padres to the tune of a 5.02 ERA (5.14 FIP). He’s proven durable the last couple seasons after missing significant time in 2023 and 2024 and can be a valuable innings-eater in the bottom half of the rotation. He won’t command top dollar, but any team who signs him will be very happy.
19. RHP Kevin Gausman
Parting with Gausman was very, very difficult for the Blue Jays. He’s been the model of consistency and durability, with the right-hander pitching at least 31 games in each season since 2021. His numbers declined this year, with a 4.51 ERA in 32 starts, though his 3.74 FIP paints a better picture. At 35 years old, he’s looking at a short-term contract. He’s still highly regarded in baseball circles and will have plenty of suitors.
20. RHP Clay Holmes
The amount of teams after Holmes at the trade deadline was massivem and had it not been for a failed physical involving a prospect, he would have been dealt to the Arizona Diamondbacks instead. He fits perfectly behind the Cubs’ elite infield defense, and considering that he is no longer eligible for the qualifying offer, his value has only increased. His market will once again be substantial.
21. OF Daulton Varsho
Varsho’s value comes with his defense in center field; he’s one of the best defenders in all of baseball. He showed growth offensively last season with the Blue Jays, with a career-high 121 OPS+. But he regressed this season, with a 76 OPS+ in 2026, including a 51 OPS+ in 41 games with the Houston Astros after being traded at the deadline.
22. INF JP Crawford
Crawford feels like a near-certainty to leave the Mariners in free agency. He’s been a mainstay in the infield the last eight seasons, with his best year coming in 2023 when he posted a 5.2 bWAR. His numbers dropped this season, as he slashed only .221/.335/.352 with a .687 OPS, 14 home runs and 40 RBI.
23. RHP Hiromi Itoh, Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters
Itoh, 29 in August, posted a 3.18 ERA in 172.2 innings. He has a seven-pitch arsenal and a fastball that touches 96 mph. He won the Sawamura Award in NPB, similar to the Cy Young Award, and teams have gotten a look at him in each of the last two World Baseball Classics.
24. RHP Dustin May
May, a former top prospect, has all the tools in his body. He has plenty of fans across baseball and there are some who believe he can still be a difference-maker atop a rotation — hence the Cardinals’ one year, $12.5 million contract for the right-hander in the offseason and the Milwaukee Brewers’ midseason trade for him. He’s since posted a 4.70 ERA in 31 starts, with a 3.63 FIP. A short-term contract once again feels likely for May.
25. OF Trent Grisham
Grisham, 29, accepted the qualifying offer last winter to stay with the Yankees for another season. While he broke out in 2025 with 34 home runs and 74 RBI, he came back down to earth with a .211/.308/.395 slash line with 18 home runs and 59 RBI this year. His 95 OPS+ puts him slightly below league-average this season. He feels like a candidate to once again sign a short-term deal in free agency.
26. 1B/OF Jake Bauers
Bauers has been a revelation in Milwaukee, and there is a real conversation to be had here about a potential qualifying offer. He’s hit .266/.389/.484 with 26 home runs and 86 RBI, and has emerged as a favorite of manager Pat Murphy, who recently noted that the slugger is being pitched to like one of the top hitters in baseball.
Honorable mentions: RHP Nick Martinez, C Carson Kelly, OF Taylor Ward, DH Joc Pederson, RHP Raisel Iglesias, OF/DH George Springer, RHP Jack Flaherty, RHP Tyler Mahle, LHP Kris Bubic,1B Ty France

item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to this season’s final edition of Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
TUESDAY
With his 25th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing broke Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
Kodai Senga became one of just 11 Japanese-born players to reach eight career saves, joining: Kazuhiro Sasaki (129), Koji Uehara (95), Takashi Saito (84), Akinori Otsuka (39), Shigetoshi Hasegawa (33), Shingo Takatsu (27), Hideki Irabu (16), Hisanori Takahashi (10), Masanori Murakami (9), and Yoshihisa Hirano (8).
Francisco Alvarez and Carson Benge each hit two doubles, marking the first time multiple Mets hit multiple doubles in a game since Ronny Mauricio and Jeff McNeil did it on July 27, 2025, in San Francisco.
WEDNESDAY
Marcus Semien hit his 15th home run of the year, giving the Mets six or more players with 15+ homers for the fifth time in franchise history after 2000 (7), 2017 (8), 2019 (6), and 2025 (6). The only teams with more 15-homer players this season were the Cubs, Reds, and Dodgers (all tied at 7). Of the Mets’ players with 15+ homers last season and this season, only two (Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto) overlap.
Juan Soto reached base four times for the 103rd time in his career, moving past Ted Williams for the third-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Mickey Mantle (121) and Jimmie Foxx (112).
Soto became the fifth Met to get intentionally walked three times in a game, after Claudell Washington (August 26, 1980), Vince Coleman (August 10, 1992), Todd Hundley (June 28, 1997), and David Wright (May 19, 2007, and July 18, 2009).
Brett Baty’s 455-foot home run tied the longest blast of his big league career, a homer off Brad Lord on August 20, 2025, in Washington.
Francisco Alvarez’s seventh-inning single registered an exit velocity of 113.7 mph. It was Alvarez’s 15th career batted ball with an exit velocity of 112+ mph, the second-most by a Met player in the Statcast era (since 2015) behind Pete Alonso, who had a whopping 130.
Alvarez, Lindor, and Baty each recorded a batted ball with an exit velocity over 110 mph, marking the first time the Mets recorded three batted balls with an exit velocity of 110+ mph in the same game since September 10, 2025, in Philadelphia.
Nolan McLean completed his rookie year with a total of 179.2 innings pitched, the most by a Mets rookie since Jae Weong Seo (188.1 in 2003), and 194 strikeouts, the third-most by a Mets rookie behind Dwight Gooden (276 in 1984) and Kodai Senga (202 in 2023).
McLean recorded his 250th strikeout in his 39th career game, tying Jacob deGrom for the fifth-fewest games by a Met to reach that milestone behind Dwight Gooden (29 games), Matt Harvey (34 games), Noah Syndergaard (36 games), and Kodai Senga (38 games).
McLean recorded his 26th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since deGrom (29) and Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
McLean became the first rookie with 20 quality starts since the Royals’ Yordano Ventura (22 in 2014). McLean’s 20 quality starts this season were tied with Sonny Gray and Cam Schlittler for fifth-most in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (22), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (22), Sandy Alcantara (21), and Michael Wacha (21). McLean also recorded his 21st start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
THURSDAY
Zac Thornton’s 63 strikeouts through 15 career games ranks fourth among Mets left-handers, behind Steven Matz (87), Bill Pulsipher (74), and David Peterson (69).
Juan Soto became the second Mets player to get intentionally walked four times in a two-game span, after Travis d’Arnaud did it while batting in the No. 8 spot ahead of Jon Niese and Bartolo Colón on June 1-2, 2014, in Philadelphia.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 63rd time this season. That ties 2013 for the most such games the Mets have had in a season in the Wild-Card Era (since 1995).
Over the franchise’s first five trips to Arlington, the Mets are still yet to lose a series on the road against the Rangers. They won two of three in 2003, won two of three in 2011, split a two-game set in 2017, won two out of three in 2024, and won two out of three again in 2026.
FRIDAY
Carson Benge became the first Mets rookie with 20+ homers and 20+ stolen bases in a season.
Benge became just the eighth player in MLB history to join the 20/20 club in their debut season, joining: Jackson Chourio (2024), Anthony Volpe (2023), Bobby Witt Jr. (2022), Julio Rodríguez (2022), Marty Cordova (1995), Ellis Burks (1987), and Mitchell Page (1977). (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Benge recorded his 43rd multi-hit game of the season, breaking Pete Alonso’s 2019 record for the most multi-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
With a pinch-hit single in the eighth inning, Brett Baty extended his career-high 18-game on-base streak. It was snapped with an 0-for-4 performance on Saturday.
Bo Bichette hit his fourth home run at Nationals Park this season, tied for the most by a Mets player in any season on the road against the Nats/Expos. His six extra-base hits trail only David Wright (7) in 2012.
Francisco Lindor didn’t notch his 300th home run on Friday night, but he did record three batted balls in a game at 107+ mph for the first time in the Statcast era (since 2015). Unfortunately for him, only one of the three resulted in a base hit.
The Mets allowed five wild pitches in a game and four wild pitches in an inning for the first time in franchise history.
SATURDAY
Jonah Tong set career highs with nine strikeouts and 19 whiffs in a game.
Mets pitchers recorded 14 or more strikeouts in a game for the 12th time this season, the fourth-most such games in a season in franchise history behind 2021 (19), 2019 (17), and 2022 (17).
With a start at shortstop, Brett Baty became the first Mets player to play six different positions in a season since Jeff McNeil in 2023.
Nate Lavender has recorded 19 scoreless appearances in his first 21 career outings, tied with Jaime Cerda, Erik Goeddel, and Daniel Zamora for the second-most by a Met behind Joe Smith (20).
In the Mets’ penultimate game of the season, their No. 8 and No. 9 hitters hit back-to-back homers (A.J. Ewing and Ronny Mauricio). The 2026 Mets had done that once before — in their first game of the season, when Carson Benge and Francisco Alvarez went deep at Citi Field against the Pirates.
The Mets clinched their sixth consecutive victory in the season series with Washington. Their record against the Nationals is 57-33 over that span.
SUNDAY
Francisco Lindor became the fifth player to hit their 300th career home run while having played at least 50% of their games at shortstop, joining Ernie Banks, Cal Ripken Jr., Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Tejada. (source: Sarah Langs on X) He is also the 11th switch-hitter to reach the 300-homer mark. (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Lindor became one of 27 players with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, and the third active player to have reached the milestone along with Andrew McCutchen and Mike Trout. He is the fifth member of that club to have played for the Mets; the others were Willie Mays, Darryl Strawberry, Gary Sheffield, and Carlos Beltrán.
Lindor became the seventh player to hit their 300th home run as a Met, joining Dave Kingman, George Foster, Gary Carter, Mike Piazza, Mo Vaughn, and Curtis Granderson.
Lindor’s 300th homer registered a 110.8-mph exit velocity, marking the third-hardest-hit homer as a right-handed batter in his career. His only harder-hit homer from the right side as a Met came on another afternoon in Washington, when he took MacKenzie Gore deep on August 21, 2025.
Ronny Maurcio became the first Met to hit three consecutive homers out of the No. 9 spot, with two on Saturday and one on Sunday. (source: SNY broadcast)
Carson Benge recorded his 14th three-hit game of the season, extending his record for the most three-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
Juan Soto holds a 1.101 OPS against the Nationals in 39 games played facing his former team. That’s the third-highest OPS for any player with at least 150 plate appearances against the Nationals/Expos, trailing only Jim Edmonds (1.198) and Todd Helton (1.114).
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Let’s talk about the rookies.
In Carson Benge, Nolan McLean, A.J. Ewing, and Zac Thornton, the Mets have four rookies with at least 1.5 bWAR*. That’s tied for the most rookies with 1.5+ bWAR* in a season in franchise history, matching the mark from 1983 (Darryl Strawberry, Carlos Diaz, Walt Terrell, and Doug Sisk).
In Benge, McLean, and Ewing, the Mets have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*. Prior to this year, they had never had as many as two such rookies in a single season. In fact, the 2026 Mets are just the third team in the modern era (since 1900) to have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*, joining:
2006 Marlins (4: Hanley Ramírez, Dan Uggla, Josh Johnson, and Aníbal Sánchez)
1989 Orioles (3: Randy Milligan, Bob Milacki, Gregg Olson)
*bWAR separated for position players and pitchers, not cumulative
Thank you for following along all year! Here’s to many more stat parties in 2027…

item.title: [MLB.com] Alonso, Arenado earn Player of the Week honors with epic finishes
item.dc:creator: Linus Lawrence
item.description: It’s never too late to make a statement. A trio of perennial All-Stars proved that point during the final week of the 2026 regular season. Pete Alonso and Nolan Arenado went on offensive tears, finishing on resounding high notes to earn the year’s last Player of the Week Awards, while Ronald Acuña Jr. received Play of the Week honors for his spectacular warning-track grab on Saturday against the Marlins. item.content:encoded:
It’s never too late to make a statement. A trio of perennial All-Stars proved that point during the final week of the 2026 regular season. Pete Alonso and Nolan Arenado went on offensive tears, finishing on resounding high notes to earn the year’s last Player of the Week Awards, while Ronald Acuña Jr. received Play of the Week honors for his spectacular warning-track grab on Saturday against the Marlins.
New York seems to awaken something within the Polar Bear. After hitting his 300th career homer back at Citi Field on Sept. 15, Alonso needed just eight more games to notch No. 307 – a jaw-dropping 471 foot shot – in a two-homer performance at Yankee Stadium on Friday night. Over his last five games in Toronto and the Bronx, Alonso reached base in 11 of his 22 plate appearances, recording five homers, eight RBIs and eight runs scored. The effort earned the first baseman his second Player of the Week Award of the second half.
Even with the Orioles’ final game of the season cancelled due to inclement weather, Alonso outpaced Yordan Alvarez to lead the American League in homers (43) and RBIs (113). He previously led the National League in RBIs with the Mets in 2022 (131), making him the first player in Major League history to lead both leagues in RBIs. He also played in every one of his team’s games for a third consecutive season.
The D-backs couldn’t complete their bid for the third NL Wild Card spot, but their veteran third baseman did just about everything he could to will them there. A game after hitting a go-ahead grand slam against the Yankees on Sept. 21, he finished a triple shy of the cycle at Coors Field on Tuesday to commence the ninth Player of the Week campaign of his career. Over the Snakes’ final six games in Colorado and San Diego, Arenado went 10-for-23 (.435) with three homers, two doubles and 5 RBIs.
With a two-run home run in San Diego on Friday, the 35-year-old notched his eighth 30-homer season and his first since 2022 with the Cardinals. The only players with more 30-homer seasons as primary third basemen are Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12) and Eddie Mathews (10).
Acuña has a complicated history with the loanDepot park outfield. This March, he clinched a World Baseball Classic championship there with Team Venezuela; but in July 2021, the right fielder tore his right ACL while leaping for a ball near the fence, sidelining him for the remainder of the Braves’ World Series campaign. On Saturday afternoon, less than 72 hours before kicking off a run at another title, Acuña proved he truly has no fear of the Miami warning track.
With no outs and a runner on first in the opening frame, Marlins slugger Heriberto Hernández lofted a Brent Suter sinker the opposite way at 101.2 mph. Acuña darted to his right at 25.6 feet per second, leapt at the fence and went tumbling to the dirt with the ball secured, giving the Braves a loud first out of the game. (Hernández went on to record his 25th homer the next day, wisely pulling the ball to left field rather than testing Acuña again.)

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Angels’ Mike Trout wants to make big change after 100-loss season
item.dc:creator: Miracle Dimwesh
item.description: Mike Trout has spent most of his career patrolling center field for the Los Angeles Angels.
